newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr finds good and bad in low inflation.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr finds good and bad in low inflation.

text.p: The Australian dollar shuddered lower Wednesday as a record low inflation result brought a long threatened cut in official rates a step closer.

Data showed the key underlying inflation rate fell through the floor of the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target range in Q2 and, with the risk of a U.S. hike seen fading for now, all that remained in the way of another easing was wages data Thursday.
"Two of three conditions for another cut have been met," said John Edwards, chief economist at HSBC Markets. "If wages data tomorrow match forecasts it should permit a move Friday."
By 4.30 pm (0630 GMT) the dollar had lurched to US$0.7373/78 from an early US$0.7389/94 and US$0.7400/05 late here Tuesday.
Traders said it found very good support at US$0.7360 and there was talk of big buying interest down at 73 cents should it re-test last week's 18-month trough of US$0.7310.

"A lot of people went short in front of the figures but there's been little but buying since," said one at a Melbourne Bank. "It's very nervous and liquidity is really poor, which makes me think the the Aussie's a buy on dips for now."
Resistance was put at Friday's rally peak of US$0.7440 and analysts saw a serious technical barrier at US$0.7475.

The selling was restrained by the fact a very low inflation result had been long flagged, as had the risk of another cut in rates. The currency has fallen around four cents since the last easing on May 23 partly in expectation of yet another.

Such an easing would take official rates below those in the U.S. for the first time since the Australian financial system was deregulated in 1983. Market rates have already anticipated the move and international investors, used to thinking of the A$ as a high yielder, have been bailing out in droves.
But this begged the question of whether a further easing had already been priced in.
"We suspect it has," said the Melbourne trader. "The dollar may come off 30 pips or so on the event but we expect bids to hold it at US$0.7330 and see it rally from there."
In any case, Australia's dramatic price improvement should support the A$ over time since relatively high inflation tends to lead to depreciation as a way of keeping exports competitive.
On the international league table Australian consumer price inflation was now below that in the U.S., Japan, Canada, the U.K., Germany, Switzerland and New Zealand, to name but a few.
The headline rate fell 0.2 percent in the June quarter taking the annual CPI to just 0.3 percent from 1.3 in Q1.

Underlying inflation rose 0.3 percent on the quarter to take annual growth to 1.7 percent from 2.1 in Q1. This was both the lowest level since the series began in 1971 and below the RBA's target band of 2-3 percent.
"The RBA can now be viewed as "overachieving" in terms of its inflation target," said Bruce Freeland, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank.
"At the very least a sub-two percent underlying inflation provides the RBA with policy leeway and the risks of erring on the expansionary side with policy are quite low at present."
He thus rated the chance of another cut at 75 percent.

An unexpectedly strong result from average weekly earnings data (AWOTE) on Thursday could yet upset calculations, although most economists looked for a moderation in wages growth to around 4.1 percent in Q2 from 4.3 the previous quarter.
If the figures conformed, the market would be on alert for a cut from Friday morning onwards.

One potential threat to the local dollar was largely removed overnight when Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan took a cautiously upbeat view on the economy in his semi-annual Humphrey Hawkins testimony. Analysts took this as implying the Fed would not be tightening U.S. policy soon.
A hike there would have further widened the U.S. dollar's yield advantage over the A$ and highlighted the diverging courses of policy in the two countries.

Greenspan's sanguine testimony prompted big rallies in stocks and bonds, both in the U.S. and here, and contributed to a jump in US$/mark. The A$ also benefited on the mark climbing to 1.34xx/xx from an already firm 1.3xxxxxxxx.

It lost ground on a stronger yen, with traders reporting heavy AUD/yen selling out of Tokyo for much of the day, to stand at 84.96/06 from 86.05/15 late Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it slipped to 57.2 from 57.4. -- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
